demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette:
Amina, a 47-year-old African American architect, first came to be seen after months of living with a sense that her life had split into a before and after. The event she traced it back to was not a natural disaster or a crime, but a brief, ordinary-looking moment that went disastrously wrong while she was driving home from work. She had been behind the wheel in her usual route through her neighborhood, thinking about revisions to a project and the errands she still needed to do, when she turned at an intersection and struck a pedestrian who stepped into the road. The collision was sudden and horrifying. In the aftermath, while people shouted and rushed toward the scene, Amina found herself holding on to fragments more than a full sequence: the sharp taste in her mouth, metallic and bitter, the sound of voices rising around her, and the sickening realization that she had caused serious injury to another person. Even when she later tried to remember the incident deliberately, the memory would not come to her in a smooth, organized way. Instead, it surfaced in broken pieces, and when it did, the taste would return so vividly that she felt as if it were happening again.

In the weeks that followed, Amina noticed that she could not summon the memory when she wanted to, yet it forced its way in at unexpected times. A passing siren, a sudden honk, or even a cupboard door slamming in her office kitchen could bring back an instant of the scene, and with it she would sometimes hear the sounds from that day in her head, as though the shouts were playing just behind her ears. She became jumpy at ordinary noises that never used to bother her. At work, where she spent long hours at her desk reviewing plans, meeting with clients, and moving between construction sites and the office, she began to react as if danger could appear at any moment. A dropped folder, a phone vibrating on the table, or the clang of equipment from a nearby site would make her flinch hard enough that colleagues noticed. She also found her attention slipping. During meetings she would stare at blueprints and realize she had read the same line several times without taking it in. She was embarrassed by how often she lost her place, as if part of her mind was still standing at the intersection.

Amina made an effort to contain the experience in the ways that made sense to her. She told herself that it could have been worse, that the other person had survived, and she repeated this privately when the guilt became too intense. But she also dwelled on what she had done wrong, replaying the seconds before the turn and searching for the moment she might have acted differently. At night she would go through small mental routines, silently checking and rechecking things in an effort to keep anything bad from happening again. She did this especially before driving, sitting for a moment with her hands on the wheel and making herself think through routes and signals in a careful sequence, as if the ritual itself might prevent another catastrophe. These habits gave her some brief relief, but they also left her more preoccupied with the event and with what it might mean about her.

What troubled Amina most was the way she had come to see herself in relation to other people. She believed someone else would not have gotten into the situation she had. The thought sat heavily on her, not as a passing regret but as a judgment about her own character and competence. She began to feel isolated and set apart from friends and even from her husband, who tried to be supportive but could not fully understand why she seemed so distant. She stopped sharing the details of her distress, partly because she did not want to burden others and partly because being around people sometimes made her feel even more like an outsider, as though everyone else moved through the world with an ease she had lost. At home she became quieter, and the version of herself that had once felt organized, capable, and assured as an architect seemed increasingly unrecognizable to her. She would look at herself in the mirror and feel that the person looking back was not the woman she had been before the accident.

By the time she sought help, Amina was tired of living in this altered state and frightened by how often she still felt on guard for danger in ordinary moments. She had come because she wanted the constant jumping, the concentration problems, the intrusive fragments of sound and taste, and the private rituals around driving to stop ruling her days. More than anything, she was afraid that the event had permanently changed who she was, and she was hoping for some way to feel like herself again without having to erase what had happened.
